add.proof:
\emph{Heavy stacks.}
For the lattice argument assume (P3).
In rank $d$, $m(\Theta)\le g^{-d}$.
By containment, $m(F^\perp)\ge\Pr[F]$.
By (I5), $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}>g^{-4}$.
For $\Pr[F]\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, the normal rank is at most three.

\emph{Prefix estimates.}

For a saturated rank $d$ lattice on $I$ with basis $B$, put the rows of a largest minor $J$ first.
Let $I_k$ be the first $k$ indices.
Let $\Theta_k$ be the integer points in the column span of $B_{I_k}$, with height $h_k$ and density $m_k$.
Invertibility gives $\Theta_d=\mathbb Z^J$. Its height is one. Point fibers give $m_d=g^{-d}$.
Saturation gives $\Theta_{|I|}=\Theta$.
For $k\ge d$, factor $B_{I_k}=YC$ with a basis $Y$ of $\Theta_k$ and integral $C$.
The maximal minors of $B_{I_k}$ scale those of $Y$ by $\det C$.
Thus $J$ remains a largest minor.
Invertible $C$ gives fibers at fixed $B_{I_k}^\top r_{I_k}$.
Extending the saturated basis $Y$ gives $G_k:=B_{I_k}^\top\mathbb Z^{I_k}=C^\top\mathbb Z^d$.
Its index is $|\det C|$.
The minor scaling thus gives $h_k[\mathbb Z^d:G_k]=h(\Theta)$.
Let $s_k$ be the order of the new row modulo $G_k$.
The new row gives index $s_k$.
Thus $h_{k+1}=s_k h_k$.
A fiber fixes the new coordinate modulo $s_k$ by reduction modulo $G_k$.
The box contains at most $\lceil g/s_k\rceil$ such values.
Conditioning there gives $m_{k+1}\le m_k\lceil g/s_k\rceil/g$.
Integer division gives $s_k\lceil g/s_k\rceil\le g+s_k-1$.
By (I1), $g^{1/b}\ge2$.
The chord of $s^{1/b}$ on $[1,g]$ has slope at least $1/g$.
Concavity gives $1+(s_k-1)/g\le s_k^{1/b}$ for $s_k\le g$.
The recursions give $m_{k+1}^{b/(b-1)}h_{k+1}\le m_k^{b/(b-1)}h_k$ for $s_k<g$.

Multiplying the rank-three prefix bounds gives $g^3m(\Theta)h(\Theta)\le\prod_k(1+(s_k-1)/g)$.
Positive powers of $1/g$ are at most $1/g$.
Evaluation at one gives coefficient sum $h(\Theta)$.
Thus $g^3m(\Theta)h(\Theta)\le1+h(\Theta)/g$.
If $m(\Theta)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, (I2) gives $h(\Theta)\le H_3$ since $\xi_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1$.
Thus $g^3m(\Theta)h(\Theta)\le1+H_3/g$.
Thus (I4) gives regularity.

\emph{Counting trimmed images.}
Take $F$ on $I\cup\{i'\}$ trimmed by a rank $d$ lattice $\Theta$ on $I$.
Fibers of $\Phi(r)=(B^\top r_I,r_{i'})$ have density at most $m(\Theta)/g$ by independence.
In full dimension $k=d+1$, retain all coordinates in the index $q$ coset.
In the other case assume $F^\perp$ has rank $1\le d'<d$, with a largest minor at $J\subseteq I$, and its restrictions to $I$ lie in the span of $\Theta$.
Put $k=d+1-d'$.
The rows $B_J$ have rank $d'$ since their column span contains the invertible minor of a basis of $F^\perp$.
Choose the final $k-1$ columns $B_2$ of $B$ to vanish on $J$, by extending an integer basis of the saturated kernel of $B_J$ to an integer basis of $\mathbb Z^d$.
The trimming form is $12/g^2$ times the squared norm of the centered column-space projection.
The invertible coordinate change preserves fibers.
Minor magnitudes are preserved by unimodularity.
Write $B_1$ for the other columns.
The restriction condition makes $\ker\Phi$ orthogonal to $F^\perp$.
Thus $\ker\Phi$ lies in the span of the differences of $F$.
Rank--nullity gives $\dim\Phi(F)=k$.
Let $V_1$ be the first $d'$ rows of a basis $V$ of $\Phi(F)^\perp$.
Pulling back $V$ gives a full-rank sublattice of $F^\perp$. Its minor at $J$ gives $|\det(B_1)_J|\,|\det V_1|\ge h(F^\perp)$.
The inequality makes $V_1$ invertible.
Image differences lie in $\ker V^\top$.
Thus dropping the first $d'$ coordinates is injective.
Saturation makes $V^\top$ map the integer lattice onto $\mathbb Z^{d'}$.
The quotient theorem gives $\mathbb Z^{d'}/V_1^\top\mathbb Z^{d'}$ for $\mathbb Z^k$ modulo the projected kernel.
The projected coset thus has index $|\det V_1|$.
Denote either coset index by $\delta$.

Use $B_2=B$ with empty $J$ and $B_1$ in full dimension.
The empty minor has determinant one.
The cylinder volume is at most $g(R_{\mathrm{tr}}g/\sqrt{12})^{k-1}\sqrt{\det(B_2^\top B_2)}$ times the unit-ball volume in dimension $k-1$.
Triangulate the image hull.
Insert all unused points by stellar subdivision.
Each $k$-simplex has volume at least $\delta/k!$ by the coset determinant.
Counting $k+1$ vertices per simplex bounds the count by $(k+1)!/\delta$ times the cylinder volume.
Since $(B_2)_J=0$, multiplying its complementary-row minors by $\det(B_1)_J$ gives minors of $B$ up to sign.
There are at most $N^{k-1}$ such minors.
Cauchy--Binet therefore gives $|\det(B_1)_J|\sqrt{\det(B_2^\top B_2)}\le h(\Theta)N^{(k-1)/2}$.
The ball volumes $2,\pi,4\pi/3$ give $(k+1)!(T_{\mathrm{tr}}/2)^{k-1}$ times volume at most $g^{k-1}\Lambda_{k-1}$ by (I3).
The count times fiber density gives $\Pr[F]\,\delta|\det(B_1)_J|\le g^{k-1}\Lambda_{k-1}h(\Theta)m(\Theta)$.
In full dimension $\delta|\det(B_1)_J|=q$.
The normal minor gives $\delta|\det(B_1)_J|\ge h(F^\perp)$ otherwise.

\emph{Regularizing a dense lattice.}
Take a saturated rank $d$ lattice of density at least $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$. We seek a regular saturated superlattice losing at most $(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ in density.
Induct downwards from rank three, where the prefix estimate already gives regularity.
For $d<3$ use the established prefix order.
Prefix densities are nonincreasing by recursion.
Choose a densest prefix fiber at each $k$.
For $k>d$, trim that fiber by $\tilde\Theta_{k-1}$ when $F_{k-1}^\perp\supsetneq\Theta_{k-1}$.
Write $F_k$ for the resulting fiber.
Trimming gives $\Pr[F_k]\ge m_k-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
If $F_k^\perp$ exceeds $\Theta_k$, its rank is at least $d+1$ by saturation.
Its rank is at most three by the density bound.
Its density meets the induction threshold $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-\operatorname{rank}F_k^\perp)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by $m_k\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The induction gives a regular superlattice $\tilde\Theta_k$ with density at least $m_k-(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
If $F_{|I|}^\perp\ne\Theta$, use its regular superlattice.

Otherwise let $j$ be the last index with $F_j^\perp\supsetneq\Theta_j$, or $d-1$ if none exists.
For $j<k<|I|$, if $s_k\ge g$ then the next coordinate is constant on $F_{k+1}$.
Its unit vector then belongs to $F_{k+1}^\perp=\Theta_{k+1}$.
It vanishes on $J$. Injectivity of restriction to $J$ rules out this unit vector.
Thus $s_k<g$.
The prefix estimate bounds $m(\Theta)h(\Theta)$ by $m_{j+1}h_{j+1}(m_{j+1}/m(\Theta))^{1/(b-1)}$.
Using $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ in the denominator raises it.
For $j=d-1$, the initial values and (I4) make this at most $\Gamma_d/g^d$.
Otherwise let $\tilde d$ be the rank of $\tilde\Theta_j$.
The normal lattice of $F_{j+1}$ is $\Theta_{j+1}$, with largest minor at $J$.
Its restriction lies in the span of $\Theta_j\subseteq\tilde\Theta_j$.
The estimate for $F_{j+1}$ trimmed by regular $\tilde\Theta_j$ gives $\Pr[F_{j+1}]h_{j+1}\le\Lambda_{\tilde d-d}\Gamma_{\tilde d}/g^d$.
The trimming bound and (I4) give $m_{j+1}\le A_{\mathrm{inv}}\Pr[F_{j+1}]$ for $m_{j+1}\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.

Monotonicity and trimming give $m_{j+1}\le\Pr[F_j]+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The larger normal rank gives $\Pr[F_j]\le g^{-d-1}$.
Now (I4) gives $(m_{j+1}/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}})^{1/(b-1)}\le P_d$.
Multiplying the bounds gives $g^dm(\Theta)h(\Theta)\le A_{\mathrm{inv}}\Lambda_{\tilde d-d}\Gamma_{\tilde d}P_d$.
By (I4), $g^dm(\Theta)h(\Theta)\le\Gamma_d$.

\emph{The modular fiber.}

For a nonzero $v$ with $v_0=0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$, omit coordinate zero and the zero entries to obtain $v_1,\ldots,v_{N_0}$.
Conditioning on the coordinates after a prefix bounds the full guessing probability by that of the prefix.
We inductively find a regular saturated lattice $\Theta$ of density $m(\Theta)>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ whose reduction contains $v_{[i]}$.
For $i=1$, use $\mathbb Z$.
Its point fibers have density $1/g$.
The modular map on the box is injective since $v_1\ne0$ and $g+1<q$.
The densest modular fiber thus has density $1/g$.
Since $1/g>\theta$, $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}<1/g$.
Now $\Gamma_1\ge1$ follows from (I4).
Thus the initial lattice of height one is regular.
Regularity bounds the induction lattice's height by $H_d$ for $d\le2$.
The rank-three estimate gives the bound $H_3$ otherwise.

Restriction to a largest minor $J$ has determinant $h(\Theta)$.
The basis bound yields $\ell_1$ norm products at most $h(\Theta)$, $2h(\Theta)$ or $9h(\Theta)$ in ranks $1,2,3$, respectively.
Lift the basis to $B$.
Cramer's rule on the span gives $y_i$ from $y_J$ by minor ratios.
Maximality bounds each magnitude by one.
The triangle inequality gives $\|y\|_\infty\le\|y_J\|_1$.

Write $v_{[i]}=Bc'$ modulo $q$.
For the next prefix take a densest modular fiber trimmed by $\Theta$, denoted by $F$.
Trimming gives $\Pr[F]>\theta-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
In particular $\Pr[F]>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
For $I=[i]$ and $i'=i+1$, the image has modular normal $c=(c',v_{i+1})$.
The coset has index $q$ because $v_{i+1}\ne0$.
In full dimension the trimmed image bound gives $\Pr[F]\le\Lambda_dg^dh(\Theta)m(\Theta)/q$.
Regularity bounds this by $\Lambda_d\Gamma_d/q$.
Condition (I5) makes this smaller than $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Thus the affine dimension is at most $d$.
Let $\Delta$ be the matrix of differences of image points.
Ellipsoid width bounds row $j\le d$ by $2R_{\mathrm{tr}}\sqrt{e_j^\top\Sigma_\Theta e_j}$.
The shape bounds this by $T_{\mathrm{tr}}\|Be_j\|_\infty$.
Last-row differences are at most $g-1$.
This is below $T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by $R_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge20$.
The maximal minors are at most $d!T_{\mathrm{tr}}^d\prod_j\|Be_j\|_\infty$ in magnitude by determinant expansion, rank $\le d$ and row bounds $\ge1$.
This is below $q$ by the basis and height bounds and (I5).
A nonzero maximal minor preserves rank modulo $q$.
Rank preservation makes the nonzero Smith factors invertible modulo $q$.
In Smith coordinates both left kernels are supported on zero rows.
Undoing the unimodular change lifts $c$ to an integer normal $u$.
Pullback by $\Phi$ gives $(Bu_{[d]},u_{d+1})\in F^\perp$.
This normal vector reduces to $v_{[i+1]}$.
The density bound gives $\operatorname{rank}F^\perp\le3$.
The lift of $v_{[i+1]}\ne0$ gives positive rank.
By the definition of $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $m(F^\perp)>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Regularization loses at most $2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The superlattice contains the lift.

Choose $z_0\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $Bz_0\equiv v_{[N_0]}\bmod q$.
The line spanned by its nonzero residue has preimage of index $q^{d-1}$.
Restriction to a largest minor $J$ makes its determinant $h(\Theta)q^{d-1}$.
By (I6) this is at most $\beta^d/d!$, using $\lfloor H_3\rfloor$ in rank three.
The closed $\ell_1$ ball of radius $\beta$ has volume $(2\beta)^d/d!$.
Minkowski gives a nonzero $B_Jz$ in this ball.
The largest-minor bound gives $\|Bz\|_\infty\le\beta$.
Since $B_Jz\ne0$, $Bz\ne0$. Its residue is nonzero by $\beta<q$.
That residue is a multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$ by the lattice choice.
Restore the zero coordinates to obtain $x$.

\emph{Application to heavy stacks.}

Take a column basis of heavy $\mathbf W$ including column zero if nonzero.
Fix the positive entries outside the basis.
Column independence gives at most one basis tuple per fiber.
Without column zero the tuple fixes only positive entries.
Otherwise $r_0$ determines $r_\star$ given the positive entries.
Each draw has $g$ residues by $g+1<q$.
The required independent draws thus have probability at most $g^{-\operatorname{rank}\mathbf W}$.
Heaviness makes this exceed $\theta$.
Since $\theta>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, also $\theta>g^{-4}$.
Hence $\operatorname{rank}\mathbf W\le3$.
Row-space membership makes $v^\top$ constant on stack fibers.
Thus $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$.
The form $\varphi_0$ gives $v_0=0$ for a kernel vector.
The modular fiber proof gives a short multiple under (P3).
Linearity puts every short multiple's nonzero residue in the kernel.
Its coordinate zero is zero as an integer by $\beta<q$.
The form equations at $x_0=0$ give $A\hat x=0$.
Padding $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ with zeros preserves the positive norm of $x$.
\emph{Witness in the row space.}
Take a nonzero usable stack of rank $d\le3$ with no kernel vector in its row space $\mathcal V$.
Let the columns of $\mathcal U$ be a basis of $\mathcal V$, with rows $u_i$.
Put $h_s=\mathcal U^\top\sigma^s(z)$ for $s\in\mathbb Z$.
The $T$-power basis makes $z$ injective on $\mathcal V$ by the kernel hypothesis.
Thus the entries of $h_0$ are base-field independent.
Frobenius preserves that independence in $h_{n/2-1}$.
Its first $d$ consecutive conjugates form a basis by the Moore criterion.
Apply a left inverse of $\mathcal U$ on the left and its transpose on the right of $W_U,W_V,\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ to obtain $\Xi_s$ at $s=n/2-1,n/2,n/2+1$, respectively. Congruence preserves symmetry.
The row and column spaces give recovery by $\mathcal U\Xi_s\mathcal U^\top$.
Reduction modulo $P$ writes the ties using the three conjugations because $\omega^{n/2}=-1$.
Applying the left inverse gives their equations $\Xi_s h_{s'}=\Xi_{s'}h_s$.
The ties give $(\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s)h_{s'}=0$ whenever $\sum_s\varrho_s h_s=0$.
Spanning gives $\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s=0$.
Thus $h_s\mapsto\Xi_s$ extends linearly to $\Xi$.
Matrix symmetry makes $\Xi(h;u,u')=u^\top\Xi(h)u'$ symmetric in $u,u'$.
The ties give symmetry in $h,u'$ by spanning.
Linearity extends cellwise Booleanity to the three matrices.
In coordinates they give $\Xi(h_s;u_j,u_j-u_0)=0$.
Spanning extends this to every $h$.
The even powers of $W_V$ make it fixed by $\sigma^{n/2}$.
Consequently $\Xi_{n/2}=\sigma^{n/2}(\Xi_{n/2})$.
Also $\Xi_{n/2-1}=\sigma^{n/2-1}(\Xi_{n/2+1})$ because the two exponents add to $n$.

The tensor is nonzero because $W_U,W_V$ determine the stack.
If $u_0=0$, take basis rows of $\mathcal U$.
All repeated entries vanish by Booleanity and symmetry.
A nonzero entry requires $d=3$.
Symmetry leaves one nonzero value $t$ on distinct basis rows.
The off-diagonal conjugate identities give $t h_s=\sigma^s(t)h_0$ for $s=n/2-1,n/2$.
Both conjugates are multiples of $h_0$ because $t\ne0$.
This contradicts the Moore basis.

Extend $u_0$ to a row basis indexed by $J$.
For $\delta\in\{0,1\}^{J\setminus\{0\}}$, choose $p_\delta$ with $u_0^\top p_\delta=1$ and $u_j^\top p_\delta=\delta_j$ at the other basis indices.
Booleanity replaces one occurrence of a repeated nonzero index by index $0$.
Symmetry leaves one entry per set $A$ of nonzero indices.
The cube entries are $\prod_{k\in A}\delta_k$.
Ordering subsets by size makes this matrix triangular with unit diagonal.
Hence $\Xi(h)=\sum_\delta c_\delta(h^\top p_\delta)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
Every $A$ occurs in a pair as $d\le3$.
The same matrix gives independence of the squares.
Set $w_\delta=\mathcal U p_\delta$.
The kernel hypothesis gives $z(w_\delta)\ne0$.
At $h_s$, the square coefficient is $c_\delta\sigma^s(z(w_\delta))$.
The conjugate identities equate this to $\sigma^s(c_\delta)z(w_\delta)$ for $s=n/2-1,n/2$.
Dividing fixes $c_\delta/z(w_\delta)$ under those powers.
Their consecutive powers generate $\sigma$.
Thus $c_\delta/z(w_\delta)\in\mathbb F_q$.

Choose a nonzero $c_\delta$ from the expansion.
Linearity on cells makes a passing test $\varrho$ vanish on $W_U,W_V$.
It vanishes on $\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ since its coefficients are in $\mathbb F_q$.
At each $h_s$, the expansion has test value $h_s^\top\sum_\delta c_\delta\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)p_\delta=0$.
Spanning gives $\sum_\delta c_\delta\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)p_\delta=0$.
Write $c_\delta=(c_\delta/z(w_\delta))h_0^\top p_\delta$.
Base-field independence of $h_0$ gives $\sum_\delta(c_\delta/z(w_\delta))\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)p_\delta p_\delta^\top=0$.
Square independence gives $\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)=0$ for this nonzero coefficient.
Booleanity gives $(w_\delta)_j((w_\delta)_j-1)=0$ for $j\in[N]$.
Substituting $w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ into each constraint test gives the constraint on $w_\delta$.
Since $(w_\delta)_0=1$, this is a witness in $\mathcal V$.

\emph{The extractor tests.}

Each candidate is checked against $S$ before output.
By bilinearity each pairing cell matrix is the outer product of the corresponding input coefficient vectors.
Applying the probes to that matrix gives the specified record update.
Up to the first mark, records represent monitor entries with guess variables set to zero, up to formal equality.
Indeed an unseen valid operand is a guess, represented by zero.
The substitution of zero commutes with the operations on expressions.
The monitor keeps only formally equal expressions at a label before the first mark.
The view result for a formally zero difference gives $W_c r=u_c$ at every $r$.
Varying $r$ forces each $W_c$ to vanish.
Thus formally equal expressions have equal stacks.

The received $G_T,\mathsf K^\alpha$ have zero cell coefficients.
(M4) excludes guesses from a good key entry.
Its nonzero stack makes it a result.
Its sketches are therefore tested.
An unrecorded old entry is a guess unused in answered calls.
At a good difference mark, cancellation requires it as an operand.
Operand records precede the result test.
Thus the tested difference has the mark stack by linearity and the record invariant.

Fix a run whose good first mark has no kernel vector in its row space.
The view makes its stack usable. Heaviness bounds the rank by three.
Symmetry makes the image of $(v_c)_c\mapsto\sum_c W_c v_c$ the row space.
Given the run, the probes give three independent uniform row-space vectors.
Their span equals the row space except with probability at most $2/q$.
The tied-form argument supplies a witness in that space.
The nonzero zeroth witness entry makes zero a pivot.
Its Boolean entries put it among the candidates.
The test is reached unless extraction has already succeeded.
Average over the runs.

\emph{Lifting.}
Take a kernel vector $v$ as in (R5).
Drop coordinate zero.
Put a nonzero coordinate first.
Scale to set $v_1=1$.
Use integer vectors of norm at most $\beta$ in each prefix whose residues are on the prefix line of $v$.
Each column is a multiple of a fixed lift of the prefix of $v$ plus a $q$-divisible column.
Multilinearity makes every four-row minor divisible by $q^3$ since terms with two lift columns vanish.
Its magnitude is at most $24\beta^4$ by determinant expansion.
It vanishes by (P4).
Thus each prefix span has dimension at most three.

Start with the basis $1$, feasible by (I6).
A nonzero bounded vector has nonzero residue by $\beta<q$.
On the line its first residue is nonzero since $v_1=1$.
Thus its prefixes are nonzero.
Return $\bot$ on a zero prefix span.

A bounded extension has its prefix in the stored span by induction.
Find integer equations for the prefix span by elimination.
With representatives in $[0,q)$, $v_{[i+1]},qe_2,\ldots,qe_{i+1}$ is a basis of the integral line lattice by $v_1=1$.
Stack the prefix-equation values of the line basis above its columns.
Column Hermite reduction gives distinct leading pivots.
Columns with zero upper parts give the extension basis below.
Its rank is at most four by the prefix span.
Write the bounds as inequalities in at most four integer coefficients.
Elimination gives integer equations for the span of found solutions.
An outside integer point violates some equation by magnitude at least one.
Each signed test is polynomial by fixed-dimensional integer programming.
At most four rounds find a basis of all bounded solutions.
Store those vectors for the next step.
Elimination of the bounded basis gives polynomial bit lengths. Applying the equations to the line basis preserves polynomial bit lengths. Hermite reduction preserves polynomial bit lengths.

Return a nonzero final vector, or $\bot$ if none exists.
Undo the permutation and restore coordinate zero.

\emph{The reductions.}
The challenge entries are jointly uniform. (R1) samples the rest independently.
Lazy injections are uniform by symmetry.
Thus (R1) has the law for $m_b$.
Independence lets (R2) precede (R1).

At a good key mark, (R3) takes the target record.
The record invariant gives $\mathsf D$ up to formal equality.
At a good difference mark, the analogous record difference represents $\mathsf D$.
By the invariant, earlier equal-label records are formally equal.
Thus no earlier difference is detected.
By (M3), the difference has nonzero value at some valid point.
The factors of $\varpi$ are nonzero there.
Thus $\varpi\operatorname{val}(\mathsf D)$ is nonzero.
The degree bound applies to this product.
The coordinate $\tau$ excludes $D$ values.
The coordinate $\varepsilon$ excludes at most $K_1+1$ values.
The grid gives $K_1+1\le n$.
Condition (P1) gives $n\le D$.
Every other coin excludes at most one value.
Schwartz--Zippel bounds failure by $d_f/(q-D)$.
By definition this is at most $\varepsilon_f$.

Encryption makes $\kappa$ independent of $r,\alpha$.
For fixed valid coins other than $\alpha$, the good-mark affine identity holds at two $\alpha$ values.
The constant term gives the plain identity $\chi\kappa$ at $r$.
Setting $\alpha=1$ makes the alpha pairs a plain expression.
The linear term gives its identity $-\mathsf D_K\kappa$ at $r$.
The view locus fixes the plain part on its fiber.
It fixes the unscaled alpha part on the alpha stack fiber.
Both values are affine in $r$ by the right exponents.
Each gradient annihilates its sector kernel.
Duality puts the gradient in the row space.
An alpha mark has zero plain stack.
Thus its plain gradient vanishes.
Formally equal expressions give the same gradients.

Condition on all but $\pi,s_{\mathrm X},\upsilon,y,\varepsilon,\Omega_{12},\zeta''$ at each probe.
By the exponent formulas, only first right coordinates contain $r$.
Their derivatives have coefficient $s_{\mathrm{leg}}$ after removing the sector factor.
Every $y_i$ term outside first left coordinates contains $\Omega_{12}$ or $\zeta''$.
The factor $1+\varepsilon\omega^{2k_1}$ has constant one.
The quotient and remainder of $\lfloor k_c/2\rfloor$ by $K_1$ are $k_2$ and $k_1$.
Thus the $\pi s_{\mathrm X}\upsilon^{k_c}y_i$ coefficient after removing the sector factor is row $W_{c,i}$.
The cell and leg indices bound the $\upsilon$ degree by $n-1$.
Apart from $\upsilon$, factors $s_{\mathrm X},y_i,\varepsilon,\Omega_{12}$ and one of $\pi,\zeta''$ occur at most once per monomial.
Thus the gradient has degree at most $n+4$.
Take a nonzero $d$-minor of the rank $d$ mark stack.
Project the first $d$ probes to its columns.
Their determinant has the minor as the coefficient of the row monomials' product at the independent points.
Its degree is at most $d(n+4)$.
By $d\le3$, $2\le n\le D$, and $K_1\ge1$, this is at most $d_f$.
The same failure estimate applies to this determinant.

On both successes, (R5) finds a kernel vector since the recovered row space is the mark row space.
The lattice argument supplies a short multiple.
The lifting algorithm returns one.
Packing gives an MSIS solution.
Any earlier successful output also solves MSIS because (R5) uses a kernel vector and a short multiple.
Conditional on each such run, the two failures cost at most $2\varepsilon_f$ by the union bound.
The reduction succeeds with probability $s_b$ over uniform challenges.
Adding the failure bound proves the good-mark estimate.

\emph{Reduction time.}
Evaluate input exponents at eight points.
Program $k\ell$ challenge entries at the chosen seed.
The product $K_1K_2=n/2$ bounds each by $n$.
Form indices are bounded by $n=(k+1)d_R$.
By (P1) and definitions, the chunk counts and lengths are $O(D)$.
The exponent formulas therefore give polynomial initialization in $D,\log q$.
For $0\le i\le N$, the QAP has $A_i,B_i\in\mathbb F_q^{<D}[X]$.
The $2(N+1)D$ coefficient slots cost $O(ND)$ advice.
Message advice uses at most $\mu$ bits.
Masking costs $O(\mu)$.
Each call updates label and exponent tables in constant time per point.
The difference test compares values at the private point.
Look up the target record.
Seed queries cost $O(d_R)$ each by lazy sampling.
Key queries take constant time in this model.

Constant-size updates per call and $L$ inputs give $O(Q+L)$ circuit nodes.
Operation coefficients are circuit constants.
Set other-sector inputs to zero.
Differentiation at the fixed points costs $O(Q+L)$.
The chain rule uses exponent derivatives to give the $r$ gradients.
The exponent formulas make this polynomial in $D,\log q$.
Elimination intersects kernels in polynomial time.
Packing uses at most $N$ coordinates.
There are at most two lifting calls.
Each is polynomial in $N,\log q$ by (P4).
The total includes advice.

\emph{The error bound.}
The quadratic coefficient of $E$ is nonnegative.
Thus $E$ is convex.
By (P5), $E(2)\le2^{-\lambda}$.
Adding (P5) gives $E(2^{\lambda+1})\le1$.
Interpolation bounds $E(u)\le u/2^{\lambda+1}$ between endpoints.
Use $u=2Q+2$.

By (M1), $\mathsf{init}$ requires a collision of formally distinct received elements of one group.
The view bound gives at most $\varepsilon_f$ per pair.
Take the union bound over $\binom{L_s}{2}$ pairs per group.

The probability of first mark $\mathsf{init}$ is at most $\sum_{s\in\{1,2,T\}}\binom{L_s}{2}\varepsilon_f$. In the experiment of Definition 3.6, $\Pr[b'=b\wedge\mathsf{Fail}]\le1/2+(f_0+f_1)/4$.
